summary: This note is a clipped Wikipedia-style overview of the United States Army's history and structure. It covers the army's organization into the Regular Army, Army Reserve and Army National Guard, and the dual-status nature of the National Guard after the Militia Act of 1903. It then traces major conflicts: the War of 1812, the Mexican border intervention and World War I, World War II, the Vietnam War, and the post-September 11 wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
one_line: Overview of the U.S. Army's structure and history, from its 1775 origins through the War of 1812, the world wars, Vietnam and the Afghan and Iraq wars.
key_facts: The War of 1812 was the second and last American war against the United Kingdom.
After taking control of Lake Erie in 1813, Americans seized parts of western Upper Canada, burned York and defeated Tecumseh, causing his Indian Confederacy to collapse.
Andrew Jackson defeated the British in the Battle of New Orleans two weeks after a treaty was signed but not ratified, and became a national hero.
Since the Militia Act of 1903, all National Guard soldiers have held dual status as National Guardsmen under state authority and, when activated, as a reserve of the U.S. Army under the President.
The task of organizing the U.S. Army commenced in 1775.
During wartime the U.S. Army was augmented by the much larger United States Volunteers, raised independently by various state governments.

American forces had been stationed in the Republic of Vietnam since 1959 in intelligence and advising/training roles, but did not deploy in large numbers until 1965, after the Gulf of Tonkin Incident.
U.S. and NATO forces invaded Afghanistan in October 2001, displacing the Taliban government, in response to the September 11 attacks.
The U.S. Army led the combined U.S. and allied invasion of Iraq in 2003.
More than 4,000 U.S. service members died in the wars (as of March 2008), and 23,813 insurgents were killed in Iraq between 2003–2011.
The United States joined World War II in December 1941 after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.
On D-Day, June 6, 1944, millions of U.S. Army troops played a central role in the liberation of Europe and defeat of Nazi Germany.
The Army Air Forces separated from the army to become the United States Air Force in September 1947.
In 1948, the army was desegregated by order of President Harry S. Truman.
In 1916, Pancho Villa attacked Columbus, New Mexico, prompting U.S. intervention in Mexico until 7 February 1917.
The United States joined World War I in 1917 on the side of Britain, France, Russia, Italy and other allies.
